topic_summaries.COP31 Climate Summit:
• The Guardian dominates coverage with extensive live blogs, analysis and commentary — framing COP31 as urgent but frustratingly incremental, while highlighting key voices like Guterres, Greta Thunberg and John Kerry
• The Independent covers similar ground but most articles are paywalled, limiting visible content; Channel 4 News takes a distinctive angle — linking Trump's Iran war and soaring fossil fuel prices to an unintended green energy boost
• BBC and Metro contribute little substantive COP31 coverage; Evening Standard and Mirror focus on Prince William's conservation work rather than the summit itself
topic_summaries.Fossil Fuel Industry Influence and North:
• GB News dominates North Sea drilling coverage, framing Labour's ban as politically inconsistent and hypocritical — highlighting rebel MPs, Falklands drilling contradictions, and an adviser's fossil fuel investments — while Channel 4 News and The Guardian treat the broader issue through an international climate lens

• The Guardian emphasises fossil fuel industry influence across multiple fronts — lobbying at Cop31, pipeline expansion, and industry-funded education — framing it as systemic obstruction to climate action

• Channel 4 News and The Guardian both cover Cop31 coal expansion critically, while GB News focuses domestically on UK drilling politics rather than engaging with the global climate summit context
topic_summaries.Energy Transition and Grid Security:
• GB News frames grid security as a vindication of gas, highlighting wind power's failures and eye-catching costs (£1m/hour); The Guardian and BBC treat the energy transition more optimistically, with the IEA declaring an "age of electricity"

• The Guardian and The i focus on barriers to EV adoption from opposite angles — Monbiot blaming industry lobbying, The i warning of rising prices if mandates are weakened — while GB News emphasises planning obstacles, rejecting a major solar farm near Blenheim Palace

• BBC foregrounds the affordability-versus-climate tension domestically, with the energy secretary conceding net zero is "under pressure"; The Guardian zooms out globally, spotlighting electrification gains in Norway, Rwanda and China
topic_summaries.Air Pollution and Extreme Weather Events:
• Evening Standard and GB News focus on immediate air pollution alerts from fog, while Metro emphasises post-Bonfire Night "code red" pollution as a distinct seasonal hazard

• The Guardian frames extreme weather through human and economic impact — a teacher's heat seizure and rising insurer subsidence claims — while BBC takes a broader food security angle via Welsh farming vulnerability

• BBC and The Sun cover fog-related accidents and oil spills as acute safety stories, keeping climate framing largely absent compared to The Guardian and The Independent's more explicit climate crisis lens
topic_summaries.El Niño: Impacts and Outlook:
• BBC and The Guardian emphasise humanitarian danger — flooding threats to Kenyan communities and maternal mortality risks in crisis zones — while Daily Mail highlights a potential benefit: fewer cold-weather deaths
• The Guardian and The Independent frame El Niño as part of a broader climate emergency ("new age of extremes," record-breaking heat), whereas Metro and The Mirror focus on the more immediate, localised threat of polar vortex disruption to UK weather
• BBC takes a future-oriented, predictive approach (North American winter forecasts, 2026 heat records), while The Guardian covers on-the-ground economic impacts such as Latin American banana producers losing income
topic_summaries.Andy Burnham and UK Climate Policy:
• GB News consistently frames Burnham's COP31 attendance negatively — emphasising taxpayer-funded travel costs, short speech duration, and half-empty halls — while the Guardian and Evening Standard focus on substantive policy announcements like the £12bn wind investment and world-first climate security role

• Channel 4 and the Guardian highlight the appointment of a Special Representative for Climate Security as a landmark moment; GB News largely ignores this in favour of travel-cost criticism and broader scepticism via the Global Warming Policy Foundation

• The Guardian offers a more nuanced debate — including a Freedland column on balancing growth with climate action — while GB News frames net zero policies purely as burdens on families and landlords

articles.raw_rss: Experts at Cop31 reveal to Nick Ferris that critical climate finance discussions are deadlocked in the wake of sweeping foreign aid cuts from wealthy nations – and share how things can move forward

For the world’s least developed countries – many of which are also suffering from debt crises, and unable to apply for loans – the core message at Cop31 is simple: much more money, supplied in the form of grants, is needed to address extreme weather resulting from climate change. 
“This is not a negotiable position for us: we did not create the climate crisis, we did not choose to have these challenges face us, and now we cannot afford to address its impacts,” says Chiku Kilembe, who is attending Cop31 as part of Malawi’s climate finance negotiating team. “For countries like ours, which has quite a severe debt situation, we really need more grants.” 
The problem is, in the wake of cuts to foreign aid from wealthy nations like the US and UK, there is much less cash available at the Cop. Last year, foreign aid fell by 23 per cent to its lowest level in a decade – spearheaded by a 56.9 per cent cut from the US – even as climate impacts have continued to escalate. 




“Climate finance is about three things: quantity, quality, and access. So if you reduce the aid budget, you are reducing the quantity,” says Debbie Hillier, policy lead on UN climate negotiations at the development charity Prosper Global. “Clearly aid reductions are bad news here.” 
The chasm between money available and money required has created something of an impasse in negotiations at Cop31. This is further complicated by the fact that the list of “Annex II” countries who are officially required to provide money in the UN system is fixed on terms devised in 1992. This means that newly-wealthy countries – including China, the UAE, South Korea and Singapore – do not officially have to provide climate finance, while the likes of Greece and Portugal are required to.

“European countries might have a lot of publicity about their cuts, but a lot of them are still doing a very good job, while a lot of very rich countries are not doing anything like what they should,” suggests Sarah Colenbrander, director of climate and environment at think tank ODI Global.

Activist Greta Thunberg reacts during a press conference at Cop31 (Reuters)
The focal point for climate finance discussions in Antalya is how exactly the world plans to meet a key target of mobilising $300bn (£227bn) in funding per year by 2035, which was agreed at Cop29 in Baku in 2024. In addition, the least developed countries are looking for clarity on what a goal to triple finance for adaptation agreed last year will look like, with climate-vulnerable countries hoping

However, sweeping foreign aid cuts from wealthy nations — including a 56.9% reduction from the US — have significantly reduced the money available, with global foreign aid falling 23% to its lowest level in a decade. articles.title: What could El Niño mean for winter weather in the US and Canada?
articles.raw_rss: El Niño winters typically bring more rain in the southern USA and drier, warmer conditions further north but the impacts on snowfall are complex.
articles.raw_meta: El Niño winters typically bring more rain in the southern USA and drier, warmer conditions further north but the impacts on snowfall are complex.
articles.jina_text:
The developing El Niño - already the strongest on record by some measures - continues to grow and could have profound effects on the weather across North America this autumn and winter.
The naturally-occurring climate phenomenon sees trade winds over the Pacific Ocean, which usually blow from east to west, weakening or reversing with warm water instead spreading eastwards.
This releases heat into the atmosphere which can drive major shifts in global weather patterns.
Impacts in the US and Canada are varied, with a greater chance of a warm and dry winter in northern areas and more risk of flooding rain further south.
There is also some evidence that El Niño can increase the likelihood of disruption to the stratospheric polar vortex which can, in turn, bring snowfall later in winter.
No two El Niños are the same and the impacts are not guaranteed - the odds are just shifted in favour of certain outcomes.






UN warns of 'supersized' El Niño as countries prepare for impact





3 September



Wet in the south




The eastward shift of warm ocean waters associated with El Niño can cause the Pacific jet stream to move south and extend eastwards, directing rain-bearing weather systems across the southern USA.
This typically leads to wetter winters during El Niño years.




Image source, BBC / NOAA
Image caption, 

The likely impacts of El Niño on winter weather vary across different parts of North America.




The latest three month forecast, external from the US National Weather Service (NWS) suggests this is a likely outcome for the winter of 2026-2027.
South-eastern states, including Florida, Georgia and the Carolinas, have the greatest chance of seeing above-average rainfall.
The El Niño winter of 1997-1998 brought significant flooding in the south-east and spun up tornadoes for Florida.



Risk of west coast floods




Image source, Caroline Brehman/EPA-EFE/REX/Shutterstock
Image caption, 

Severe flooding hit Long Beach, California in February 2024.




California could well find itself in the firing line with forecasts suggesting a wet winter is likely. 
Governor Gavin Newsom has already declared a state of emergency, external ahead of anticipated floods and mudslides.
Areas scarred by recent wildfires are particularly susceptible, with the effects of climate change exacerbating the risks.
Many past El Niños have been wet here, with winter 2023-2024 bringing relief from drought. However this is not always the case. In the strong El Niño of 2015-2016, California actually had below-average rainfall.
Coastal erosion and large waves could be worsened by a rise in the overall sea level driven by so-called Kelvin waves.
This is where ocean water which sloshes eastwards across the Pacific due to El Niño reaches the west coast of the Americas, where it can travel no further.
It causes a large-scale wave which then spreads along the coast over a period of weeks and months, raising sea levels by 15cm (6in) or more.

Full SummaryUnited Nations Secretary-General António Guterres called for immediate and drastic fossil fuel emission cuts during his final climate summit in Turkey to prevent catastrophe. Guterres warned that climate change drives geopolitical instability and poverty while urging wealthy nations to provide promised finance to vulnerable countries.
 The world must immediately and drastically cut fossil fuel emissions to avert the most catastrophic effects of climate change, United Nations Secretary-General António Guterres said Friday at his final climate summit, urging the world to “follow the science” and face hard facts.
“You cannot build peace on a burning planet," Guterres told reporters, stressing that climate change is central to the U.N.'s work because it contributes to geopolitical instability by driving hunger and displacement, pushing countries into debt and fueling competition for land and water.
“You cannot eradicate poverty when climate disasters keep throwing people back into it,” he added. “You cannot promise young people a better future while destroying the natural systems on which that future depends. And you cannot speak seriously about justice when those who did least to cause this crisis suffer first and worst.”





World leaders meeting in Turkey for the annual U.N. climate talks are trying to reach consensus on concrete actions to address climate change — which is fueling more intense and deadly heat waves, droughts, floods and other disasters — and help countries at greatest risk, including island nations that also are losing land to rising seas.

Fight the climate crisis or go for growth? There is a way Burnham can do both 

Jonathan Freedland



The environmental and economic dilemmas he faces are formidable but, with a bold plan, he could set an example for leaders around the world




For politicians of the centre-left especially, it’s the great dilemma of the age. How do you do what everyone can see is essential to save the planet from boiling – even as your voters demand action to get the economy growing and to make life more affordable? Plenty of activists will tell you there’s no contradiction, that tackling the climate crisis makes economic as well as ecological sense and, in the long term, you know they’re right. But you don’t live in the long term. You’re running the government right now and facing several unavoidable, binary choices.
Andy Burnham is a prime example. This week, he addressed the Cop summit in Antalya, promising “a new era of British leadership” in the struggle against global heating. It’s important to him to talk that way: his political strategy relies on shrinking the appeal of the Green party, whose electoral success earlier this year helped remove his predecessor. But talk only takes you so far. Eventually the words have to be matched by action.



That’s where things get tricky. Last month Burnham’s government approved the Jackdaw gasfield in the North Sea, dismaying climate activists. Soon there will have to be a decision on Rosebank, the much bigger proposed new oilfield northwest of Shetland. There are also signs that ministers are preparing to weaken the targets set for the car industry to shift to electric vehicles. And this week, the chancellor, John Healey, declared himself fully “behind building a third runway at Heathrow”. Small wonder that campaigners are talking of hypocrisy and the government’s “crumbling” credibility.
What is Burnham to do? He has Healey in one ear, telling him that a thriving airport is an engine for economic growth, doubtless alongside the oil, gas and car industries. And in the other he has the climate scientists, reminding him that global carbon emissions are at record levels and the planet is getting hotter every year. What option does he have, except to keep putting off the moment of choice, buying himself time by saying, for example, that Rosebank is a “quasi-legal decision” that cannot be hurried?

‘You cannot build peace on a burning planet,’ UN chief tells Cop31 in farewell speech


António Guterres says climate action central to every aspect of UN’s work, as leaders depart Cop31 and talks go on




Tackling the climate crisis is central to all of human life and must be at the forefront of global governance, the outgoing UN secretary general has said in an emotional farewell address at the Cop31 climate summit.
“You cannot build peace on a burning planet,” António Guterres said at his final climate press conference as secretary general on Friday. “You cannot eradicate poverty when climate disasters keep throwing people back into it. You cannot promise young people a better future while destroying the natural systems on which that future depends.”

Guterres has been the most forthright secretary general yet on the subject of the climate, returning to it again and again to castigate fossil fuel companies and recalcitrant governments.
He leaves office at the end of December and his successor is still unknown after Donald Trump tried to interject his preferred choices into the process. There are widespread fears that the next incumbent will downplay the climate crisis in favour of other issues.


In a clear message to his successor, Guterres spelled out why the UN must continue to place the climate at the top of the global agenda. “Climate change does not stay in its lane,” he said. “It drives anger and displacement around the world. It wipes out development gains built over decades. It pushes countries deeper into deficit. It aggravates competition for land and water.
“It fuels instability. And increasingly, it threatens the very existence of communities and countries. For all these reasons, I have never viewed climate action as just one of many other issues. Climate action is central to every aspect of the work of the UN.”
Guterres was one of the few world leaders left at Cop by Friday afternoon as most of the more than 90 who had attended returned to their capitals, leaving negotiators to get down to tackling issues such as the electrification of the global economy and a just transition out of fossil fuel industries for workers.

The Australian prime minister, Anthony Albanese, flew out after hosting a meeting between major international investors and Australian renewable energy companies, followed by a meeting with Taneti Maamau, the president of the low-lying Pacific nation of Kiribati. California governor Gavin Newsom endorses global fossil fuel phaseout


Newsom is the most prominent US politician at Cop31, a process the Trump administration continues to boycott




The leader of the world’s fourth biggest economy, California governor Gavin Newsom, has explicitly endorsed a global phase out of the fossil fuels that drive climate breakdown.
Newsom told the Guardian that California is “100%” behind the efforts of the so-called Santa Marta coalition, a group of more than 50 countries that includes many of the world’s largest economies, to transition away from oil, gas and coal toward solar, wind, batteries and other non-carbon energy sources.

Speaking at the Cop31 UN climate summit on Thursday, Newsom said: “When you have a product that is obviously superior, which clean energy is for the climate and the economy, why wouldn’t you make that shift as quickly as possible?”
As the head of America’s most populous and economically powerful state, Newsom is the most prominent US politician at Cop31, a process the administration of US president Donald Trump continues to boycott.






Cop31 as it happened: ‘You cannot build peace on a burning planet’, warns UN chief Guterres in final climate summit speech

Read more
Newsom, a Democrat, is widely expected to run for president in 2028. His statement raises the possibility that the US, the world’s biggest economy and largest historical emitter of planet-warming gases, could join the Santa Marta coalition if he wins the presidency two years from now.
More than 80 countries wanted last year’s COP30 to begin to develop a global “roadmap” to phase out fossil fuels. A handful of petrostates led by Saudi Arabia blocked that effort, relying on the disputed notion that decisions at UN climate summits can only be made by consensus. Undaunted, countries favoring a roadmap met in April in Santa Marta, Colombia, to begin designing a phase out on their own.
“Love it,” Newsom said of the challenge that this Santa Marta “coalition of the willing” is posing to the US and other states intent on keeping the world burning fossil fuels.

The super El Niño is officially here, NOAA's Climate Prediction Center announced Thursday.
Water temperatures in the Pacific Ocean reached the threshold needed for the designation, rising to at least 0.5 of a degree Celsius (0.9 of a degree Fahrenheit) above average for three consecutive months. The natural climate pattern has been in effect since late spring, leading to historic flooding in the southern U.S. and impacting massive ocean swells along coastlines.
But the U.S. hasn’t seen the worst of its impacts yet, with more coming through the spring. 
“El Niño continues to strengthen, with a strong-to-very strong El Niño likely through January-March 2027,” NOAA said.





open image in gallery
It’s official. The super El Niño is here, with impacts lasting through next spring. Rainy weather has already hit some areas of the US (Getty Images)
This weekend, Americans from coast to coast are facing wet weather. A Pacific storm is expected to dump more rain on the West as a nor’easter affected by the subtropical jet stream continues to hammer the Northeast.

Full SummaryClimate action for vulnerable nations must include agricultural subsidy reform to ensure a just rural transition, according to Carlos Alvarado. The goal is to redirect the $800 billion spent on global agricultural subsidies toward sustainable practices without undermining food security or farmer livelihoods.
Climate action for the most vulnerable countries cannot be effective without also factoring in agriculture. It is the backbone of many economies and the foundation of food and nutrition security.
The sector is simultaneously among the most important and the most exposed for those on the frontlines of rising temperatures.
And yet many of the most climate-vulnerable countries are also following a similar path set by high-income countries, using public support to inadvertently perpetuate environmentally damaging agricultural practices and inputs, while not supporting smallholder farmers nor guaranteeing nutritious food for people.





As climate negotiators seek to advance the Belem-Antalya Mechanism (BAM) for a just transition at the UN’s Cop31 talks amid a challenging economic context, climate-vulnerable countries must be supported to rethink agricultural subsidies and support to build long-term resilience.
The challenge is not to cut subsidies, but to redirect them without undermining farmers' livelihoods or food security, or in other words, bringing about a just rural transition.

articles.title: Climate action discussed at youth COP meeting
articles.raw_rss: School children gather to discuss climate issues to coincide with the COP31 conference in Turkey.
articles.raw_meta: School children gather to discuss climate issues to coincide with the COP31 conference in Turkey.
articles.jina_text:
School children are taking part in an event aimed at inspiring climate action, to coincide with the COP31 international climate conference in Turkey.
Hosted at the Kingston Maurwood campus, the first Dorset-wide Youth COP has brought children from 14 schools together to discuss issues including future careers.
Maria Clarke, of Dorset Local Nature Partnership, said young people should be "given a voice" over dealing with climate change.
A Dorset COP 2026 event is also being held on Saturday as world leaders and delegates gather at Antalya in Turkey for the COP31 climate summit.
The Dorset Youth COP event includes discussions about how young people feel about climate change as well as a panel session introducing them to the range of jobs and careers in the climate and energy sectors.
Maria Clarke, of Dorset Local Nature Partnership, said: "Young people are inheriting the climate and ecological emergencies that previous generations have created and need to be given a voice in jointly developing and implementing the solutions to these issues." 
"The Youth COP aims to raise awareness, inspire and support them to take action now and into the future."







More stories from Dorset





Watch the latest episode of South Today





Listen to the latest news from Dorset














The main Dorset COP 2026 event takes place on Saturday also at the Kingston Maurward Campus near Dorchester. 
The fourth annual event brings together community groups, environmental organisations, experts and political leaders.
The programme will explore how Dorset can respond to climate change, nature loss, food resilience, pollution and other environmental challenges.
The programme will also feature an exhibition of over 30 local organisations and a Question Time-style panel bringing together Dorset MPs, council leaders and independent climate experts. 
Giles Watts, chair of Dorset CAN said the event's focus was on making "a lasting positive impact" on climate and nature local areas.
"We want to bring people together, listen to different perspectives and energise local communities and politicians to act more quickly on the pressing challenges we face," he added.

From 36m ago


“You cannot build peace on a burning planet,” the UN secretary-general, António Guterres, has warned in a final speech. The outgoing diplomat, and outspoken climate activist, celebrated the progress made in his last decade doing the job while warning of the wide gap between what science demands and politics deliver.
“You cannot build peace on a burning planet,” he said. You cannot eradicate poverty when climate disasters keep throwing people back into it. You cannot promise young people a better future while destroying the natural systems on which that future depends. And you cannot speak seriously about justice when those who did least to cause this crisis suffer first and worst.”
Guterres backed the Turkish and Australian co-hosts push for electrification – caveating that it must be clean – and praised the Cop30 presidency’s roadmaps on transitioning away from fossil fuels and on deforestation. He also called for confronting the disproportionate influence of the fossil fuel lobby.
“The future of our planet cannot be negotiated on the terms of those profiting from its destruction.”

The NSW premier has shown Trumpian disdain for the damage burning coal is causing – and it may backfire on him

Bob Brown


Chris Minns has gone out of his way to help ban peaceful protest in Newcastle, the world’s biggest coal port. Voters will remember in March 
 
 




We know that El Niño climate patterns are supercharged by the burning of fossil fuels. In Europe, more than 50,000 people died of intolerable heat this year. And yet, in September the premier of New South Wales, Chris Minns, oversaw the largest coalmine expansion in the state’s history.
Coal from that operation in the Hunter Valley will inevitably increase global warming after it is exported through Newcastle and then burned overseas. Newcastle, the world’s biggest coal port, has become the target of a restless population, particularly of young Australians, alarmed by global warming.

The protest organisers, a group called Rising Tide, are impressive. Their colourful, peaceful and remarkably safe tactics have seen the flow of massive coal-laden ships slowed and sometimes halted as hundreds of kayaks and other craft have formed flotillas in Newcastle’s Hunter River port. As the climate emergency has grown, so have the thousands of people joining Rising Tide’s annual demonstrations.


This week, Minns wrote an endorsement for Newcastle’s lord mayor Gavin Morris’s move to ban protesters from council-owned land. The motion was to prevent any event or protest organised by Rising Tide or associated groups or individuals on council-owned land “now and into the future”. Minns’s letter was used to influence the Morris motion to pass 7-6. Three Greens councillors voted against the motion, while Labor councillors were split. A Liberal councillor said it was an opportunity to rid the city of the “scourge” of Rising Tide. Police were called to settle the ensuing uproar in the council chambers.

Morris fuddled his way through media questions next day, explaining that the ban extended beyond Rising Tide to other like-minded or supportive protesters, even including pro-Palestinian demonstrators. He also revealed that he has had calls from around the world condemning his action.

View image in fullscreen
An Edwardian home’s bay window being held up by props owing to subsidence in Palmer’s Green, north London. Photograph: EDIFICE/Alamy


UK’s biggest insurer hit by rise in subsidence claims after record hot summer


Increase reported by Aviva after Hastings Direct said claims were up 140% in August and Axa said it had been a ‘surge year’




The UK’s largest insurer has been hit by a rise in subsidence claims after an extremely hot summer left households across the country grappling with the fallout from the growing climate crisis.
Aviva said on Friday it had experienced the jump amid an industry-wide surge in households filing subsidence claims with their insurers to cover repairs, which typically are needed to address cracks, sloping floors, and off-kilter doors and windows.

It follows two record hot summers in the UK; August this year was the joint hottest month ever recorded around the world. Drier summers cause the ground under houses to shrink, which undermines a property’s foundations. It then expands in wetter winters, which can further damage homes.







UK subsidence claims surge after hottest summer on record

Read more
Aviva experienced a “peak subsidence period” between July and September, with claims continuing into October, its chief executive, Amanda Blanc, told Bloomberg in an interview on Friday. Aviva would not provide any further detail on the scale of the increase in claims.
Blanc said homeowners could reduce the risk of subsidence by keeping a close eye on drains, pipes and gutters, and fixing any leaks that could affect the ground under homes. “It’s about managing trees and plumbing,” she said.
A number of fellow insurers have also experienced a rise in claims in recent months. Hastings Direct said it received record subsidence claims in August, up 140% compared with a year earlier. Axa, one of the UK’s biggest home insurers, has said it has been a “surge year” for subsidence.


The value of claims have also hit a record high. The average subsidence claim in the UK hit a high of £20,000 between April and June, more than £2,000 higher than a year earlier, according to the Association of British Insurers. Insurers paid out £72m for domestic subsidence claims, compared with £60m in the same period last year.
Millions of homes are at risk of subsidence because of the worsening climate crisis, according to the British Geological Survey, which estimates that up to 11% of UK homes – more than 4.2m houses – could be at risk by 2070. Older properties with shallow foundations and those built on clay-rich soil are facing the biggest threat, with areas including London, Essex, Kent and areas around Oxford among the most vulnerable.

Cop31 live – latest updates  




More than 100 corporations and industry groups linked to fossil fuel interests have sent delegations to the UN climate talks in Turkey, according to an analysis.
The Cop31 climate summit in Antalya is thought to be the largest ever in the three decades of the annual gatherings, with more than 92,000 delegates registered to attend talks aimed at shifting the world away from the fossil fuels that are dangerously overheating our planet.

This swell of people includes numerous groups that support or are influenced by coal, oil and gas interests, the review has found. In total, 103 groups with a track record of obstructing climate action or furthering fossil fuel interests are at Cop31, according to the Kick Big Polluters Out coalition, which comprises about 450 environmental organisations.


The groups include 60 fossil fuel industry bodies, 16 financial companies that fund fossil fuels, six industrial agriculture and foods products groups, three big tech groups and 20 cross-sector organisations.
Among the largest delegations are the International Emissions Trading Association, which has 29 people at Cop and has been accused of helping provide legitimacy to fossil fuel companies, BNP Paribas, HSBC and Amazon. The oil firm Exxon has a delegation of 13 people in Antalya, TotalEnergies has five and BlackRock, another big financier of fossil fuel projects, has five.
These delegations outnumber the national delegations sent by some of the countries most vulnerable to climate impacts. Nepal, which suffered a devastating, deadly glacier collapse this summer that has been linked to global heating, has just a sixth of the number of delegates of these groups.
Prakash Dalal from Pro Public/Friends of the Earth Nepal said: “Big polluters have caused loss of livelihood, emotional damage, trauma and survival challenges for our people.
“We cannot tolerate the disproportionate space given to them compared to civil society and our country delegations.”
Large numbers of fossil fuel lobbyists have long been a feature of the UN climate talks, with one in every 25 participants at last year’s summit in Brazil a fossil fuel lobbyist. Environmental advocates have called for better transparency and conflict of interest disclosures for those attending, and influencing, the climate talks.

A super El Niño brings startling changes for marine life on California coast: ‘like nothing we’ve ever seen’


Water temperatures are climbing the charts, high tides are swallowing the shoreline and vital parts of the food web that feed ocean diversity are disappearing




On a picturesque autumn afternoon last week, the beaches of California’s Monterey Bay were teeming with life and death.
A cadre of shorebirds charged and retreated in a synchronized dance with the raging surf. Nearby, the receding tides had deposited lifeless bundles of feathers and bone, tangled in piles of glistening kelp. Swollen sea lion carcasses, their teeth bared in a quiet grimace, dotted the sand as beach picnickers and dog walkers enjoyed the warm, cloudless day.

The effects of a historic El Niño have officially reached Monterey Bay, according to scientists, and the mortality on display here may be a grim harbinger of more to come. The waters that hug California’s central coast are already undergoing startling changes.


The climate phenomenon, defined by unusually warm equatorial ocean conditions, is rapidly heating and expanding parts of the Pacific. Water temperatures are climbing off the charts, from the ocean’s depths to its surface. Record-smashing high tides are swallowing more of the shoreline. Plus, vital parts of a vibrant food web that feeds ocean diversity are disappearing, starving scores of species throughout the system.


These changes are compounding the impacts from the climate crisis and extreme marine heatwaves that have already stressed ocean ecosystems and their inhabitants.
“It is like nothing we’ve ever seen,” said Dr Jono Wilson, the science director for The Nature Conservancy’s oceans program. “We just are trying to figure out how to wrap our heads around the sheer scale of this event.”
Visual reports from divers, underwater cameras, and beach-goers have showcased how deeply underwater environments are changing. Waters clouded with nutrients cleared as they warmed, and an unusual array of visitors arrived from the southern seas.
The central coast has played host to schools of halfmoon fish that ventured far past their southern California range, translucent winged comb jellyfish generally spotted on dives near Hawaii, and Humboldt squid that are usually found in the eastern equatorial Pacific. Whale sharks common in the Sea of Cortez were seen in Malibu and juvenile garibaldi fish – brilliantly orange speckled with glowing electric blue splotches – were seen for the first time in Monterey Bay.

El Niño stokes a higher risk of death in childbirth for millions of women in the world’s harshest crisis zones, midwives have warned.
Converging waves of weather – floods, cyclones and extreme heat – forecast to peak in the coming months will prove fatal for many, especially pregnant women, who face being cut off from hospital when in labour.

About 15 million babies are due to be born in November and December in countries rated as high risk for El Niño – that represents two in every three births worldwide.
They include Nigeria, Chad, Central African Republic, South Sudan, Somalia and Afghanistan, which already have some of the world’s highest maternal and newborn death rates. About 260,000 women die in pregnancy and childbirth every year, mostly of avoidable causes, with sub-Saharan Africa carrying 70% of the burden.
“If you’re female, pregnant, socially deprived and in a climate catastrophe zone, the odds are stacked against you before you even conceive,” said Anna af Ugglas, chief executive of the International Confederation of Midwives (ICM) today. “El Niño is coming on top of other health risks – and for many this will become the difference between life and death.”


View image in fullscreen
A mother and baby in a clinic in Chad, which has a high maternal and newborn death rate. Photograph: Martin Bertrand/Hans Lucas/AFP/Getty Images
In Bangladesh, maternity teams are braced for floods.
“Childbirth does not stop during a cyclone, flood, heatwave or landslide,” said Christine Ewoi Eloto, a midwife mentor in the Rohingya refugee camps of Cox’s Bazar in Bangladesh. “Even a short delay in reaching a facility during an obstetric emergency can cost a mother or her baby’s life.
“During previous flash floods and landslides, women could not reach health facilities. Roads were submerged and our vehicle got stuck.”
In southern Malawi, a heatwave is keeping women from antenatal care. A failed rainy season has left farming families unable to afford bus fares to a clinic – so issues go untreated.
“At present we’re facing temperatures above 40C most of the week,” said midwife Judith Mgogo. “Antenatal attendance is expected to be low since women cannot travel in such hot weather. We are having electricity blackouts every day.”
When electricity fails, midwives deliver babies in sweltering wards or by torchlight, said midwife Madalitso Ben Malekano, of Phalombe district. “Extreme heat is causing dizziness and fatigue in many women – and that includes myself.”
Previous strong El Niño events have left more than 4 million Malawians short of food. “There will be malnutrition, which will lead to low birthweight babies and heavy maternal bleeding – a consequence of anaemia,” said Ben Malekano.

The UN’s annual climate summit is known for being arcane, long-winded and frustrating. On Wednesday, however, Turkey brought a dash of Eurovision-style glamour to proceedings.
The hosts of the talks, held in the historic Mediterranean city of Antalya, decided to blast assorted world leaders, dignitaries and other delegates with Let’s Cop, a bona fide floor-filler that includes the lines: “Bring down the heat, make it drop. One world, one call, let’s Cop.”

This banger followed a lengthy display of whirling, high-octane dancing by performers in traditional Turkish clothing, and a period of interpretive performance featuring a woman dressed as some sort of shrub and a troupe entangled in a costume formed of plastic waste. But it was Let’s Cop that was the most intriguing.


I’ll tell you why, after today’s climate headlines.
Essential reads
 
 
‘The world we know is over’ without urgent climate action, leaders tell Cop31  
 
Oil slicks seen from space: the devastating impact of boat strikes on fragile Gulf ecosystems  
 
Bird flu has caused catastrophic die-offs – could a wave of extinctions follow?  
In focus


View image in fullscreen
Dancers of the Fire of Anatolia showcase traditional folk dances. Photograph: Dogukan Keskinkılıç/Anadolu/Getty Images


On hearing Let’s Cop, the immediate, uncharitable, question about this banger was, is this AI? My intrepid colleague Graham Readfearn secured the following answer from the Turkish hosts: “The song’s melody and lyrics were written by a professional musician, while AI tools were used in the composition and production process.”
Whatever that cryptic explanation means, the shades of Eurovision introduced by Let’s Cop were a welcome fillip for a climate conference that has been bedevilled by troubled logistics and a distinct lack of progress – or even direction – on the central priorities of ending the fossil-fuel era and adequately supporting the countries most vulnerable to climate disasters.
There is still a long way to go in Cop31, which is slated to finish next Friday. But so far, to extend the metaphor: what would the Eurovision-style scores be?
Well, Turkey and Australia jointly oversee this Cop and yet each are significant consumers of fossil fuels and are actively increasing their polluting activities even as the climate conference is under way? Nul points.
Countries are cutting their emissions far too slowly to avoid disastrous climate breakdown and yet talk of ending fossil fuels is still considered a bit too risque? Nul points.

articles.jina_text:

World is now in ‘age of electricity’, energy agency chief says


Exclusive: Fossil fuels no longer dominant energy source, IEA leader says, as summit considers electrification pledge




The world has left behind the age of coal, oil and gas and is now firmly in “the age of electricity”, the world’s leading energy economist has said.
Fatih Birol, the executive director of the International Energy Agency (IEA), said more than twice as much electricity generation would be added to the global economy in the next decade than in the last, as countries scramble to secure their energy supplies against fossil fuel price volatility and supply shocks, such as the Iran war.

Transport is being electrified at an unprecedented rate: outside China, sales of electric cars have risen by 60% in the last nine months, the IEA has found. The growth of AI datacentres is also spurring electricity generation, as is the rapid growth in air conditioning, according to Birol, as heatwaves grow more intense and more frequent under rising global temperatures.







The planet ‘is being killed’, Greta Thunberg tells Cop31 climate summit

Read more
“We will still use oil and gas, but the dominant source of energy is becoming electricity,” Birol told the Guardian in an interview at the Cop31 UN climate summit in Turkey. “One staggering number [is that] in the last 10 years, the world has added about 5,000 gigawatts of electricity. And we expect, in a very conservative way, in the next 10 years, about 12,000 gigawatts, more than two times more than what we had in the last 10 years.”
Governments from 185 countries are meeting this week and next in Antalya for the annual talks, where the turn to electrification in place of fossil fuels is one of the key topics. A resolution to derive 35% of final energy worldwide from electricity by 2035 is on the table, which if it succeeds, could be one of the most important ways of achieving the needed decarbonisation of economies by mid-century.
Electricity now fulfils about a quarter of most energy needs while three-quarters of final energy worldwide is supplied by fossil fuels, mostly for transport, heating and industrial uses. Global electricity was increasingly generated by renewable sources and that process would speed up even faster over the next decades, Birol said.

Owning an electric car, driving an electric motorbike taxi, riding scooters – we speak to people in Oslo, Kigali and Shanghai about their everyday routines




The race to electrification has emerged as a key theme of this year’s UN climate summit: increasing the use of electricity – particularly from clean sources – has the potential to improve daily life for people around the world.
The summit’s co-hosts are now trying to get countries to promise to increase their electricity use to 35% of all energy used by 2035. The global figure currently stands at 23%, but some countries are already striding ahead. As 100,000 delegates, negotiators and world leaders thrash out the details in Antalya, Turkey, the Guardian spoke to three people in Norway, Rwanda and China to find out what life looks like in more highly electrified countries.

An office worker in Oslo, Norway


View image in fullscreen
‘I mostly use my electric car on weekends,’ says Unni Berge, who lives in ‘a rather energy-efficient flat’ in Oslo with her husband and two sons. Photograph: Norwegian EV Association
Norway is a world leader in the race to 100% electrification. In September, a record 98.81% of new cars sold were electric, and hydropower produces 90% of all electricity. But with rapidly rising energy demands, including from new datacentres, authorities warn that the country could soon face a power deficit and higher energy prices.


Unni Berge, 47, lives in Oslo with her husband and two teenage sons and works as the head of communications at the Norwegian EV Association. She describes how electricity features in a typical day:
“I use electricity in my three-bedroom flat and I have district heating [where heat is transported around a local network from a centralised source rather than individual boilers to heat homes and buildings]. For electricity we are connected to the Norwegian central grid, which is mainly hydropower.
“I live in a rather energy-efficient flat, so our electricity bills are comparatively low. In October, we spent 730 Norwegian kroner [£57] on electricity for our apartment, and in September it was 500 kroner.


View image in fullscreen
Electric cars charging at a station in Alta, in Finnmark, northern Norway. Nearly 99% of new cars sold in Norway in September were electric.  Photograph: Salwan Georges/Washington Post/Getty Images


“I go to work by bus. Almost all the buses in Oslo are fully electric. I also have an electric car, but driving in the middle of Oslo for work is not an option because we have a lot of restrictions on cars in the city centre. In my street, the bus comes every fifth minute, so I don’t have to plan. I go outside and a bus comes.
“I mostly use my electric car on weekends. A lot of the trips are driving to sports activities with my two children, who are 18 and 15. I also train a handball team, so I use it to go to a lot of handball matches and tournaments.

articles.title: How much air pollution is in your London area? Interactive map gives real-time level amid weather alert

articles.jina_text:
Londoners have been warned of dangerously high levels of air pollution this week, with online data showing that levels could result in “serious health effects”.




Periods of dense fog combined with low wind allowed harmful particles to build up across the capital, with a high air pollution alert in effect in London on Tuesday on advice from forecasters at Imperial College London.








Vulnerable residents in particular were urged to take care, in the fourth high air pollution alert issued by Mayor Sadiq Khan so far this year.




Forecasters say that smoke from Bonfire Night and Diwali fireworks, as well as wood burning, are likely to have contributed to the high levels.


Fog shrouding the London Eye
AFP/Getty




Since Tuesday, levels have fallen across the capital - but some parts of London still have levels which could cause moderate health concerns for people who are unusually sensitive to air pollution. 




An interactive map, created by the World Air Quality Index Project, is a real-time source of air quality information across the city. 




The site, which covers major cities around the world, collates data from more than half a million air quality monitoring stations across the planet, in a bid to raise awareness of air pollution.











According to the site’s data, between Sunday and Tuesday, much of the capital was in the “unhealthy” zone - meaning everyone could begin to experience health effects, and members of sensitive groups could experience more serious health effects.




The site suggests that active children and adults, and people with respiratory disease, should avoid prolonged outdoor exertion during such conditions.


Air Quality Index scores recorded in London this week
World Air Quality Index Project,


Much of London was in the 'unhealthy' zone earlier this week
World Air Quality Index Project,




Some London boroughs were covered by the highest levels of pollution, according to air pollution maps provided by the Apple Weather app. 







The City of Westminster, Wandsworth, Lambeth, Merton, Ealing, Brent, Tower Hamlets, Greenwich and Bexley were all rated 10 earlier this week, with most of the other boroughs being rated 8 or 6, including Croydon, Richmond upon Thames and Kensington and Chelsea.




North London had somewhat clearer air, according to the maps, with boroughs including Haringey and Enfield mainly being rated 2 or 4. 


A map of air pollution in London from earlier this week
Apple Weather




Particularly foggy conditions caused disruptions at London's airports on Monday, with several flights from Heathrow and London City airports cancelled.

An indigenous climate activist who is taking the Australian government to the UN human rights committee over its coal and gas exports stood alongside Greta Thunberg at Cop summit to demand Anthony Albanese “stop speaking and start listening.”
Draped in traditional dress in front of a media throng, Rikki Dank, a Gudanji and Wakaya traditional owner, delivered an impassioned plea to Albanese to listen to “the Australian people when they say no more new coal, oil and gas”.







‘I was home alone when the glacier collapsed. My mum called and told me to run’ – This is climate breakdown

Read more
Albanese on Thursday defended his major speech at the opening of Cop31 after facing criticism for omitting the phrase “fossil fuels”.
Australia is the president of the two-week negotiations at Cop31 being held in Antalya, Turkey. A key push from the two hosts is to garner support for a “35 by 35” pledge for 35% of end-use energy to be from electricity by the year 2035.
The UN secretary general, António Guterres, and several countries are pushing the two hosts to also progress a proposal from last year’s Cop president, Brazil, to have countries develop roadmaps to transition away from fossil fuels.
Squeezed into a corner of the vast Cop31 media centre, Thunberg was flanked by Dank and other climate advocates, including a Nepalese MP who had helped rescue people from a landslide that followed an August glacier collapse that killed more than 1,500 people.
Thunberg said: “It is more clear than ever in spaces like these that the situation could not be less under control. The planet is not dying, it is being killed.






Datacentres are deeply unpopular. Has Sweden made one we can all love?

Read more
“And we know by who. And it is being killed by the very same people often thought to come to our rescue.”
She said it was “common sense” that Australia needed to take greater action on climate change.
Dank is one of 10 Australians behind a complaint before the UN human rights committee – known as the Hard Truths case – that claims the Australian government has failed to protect them from climate pollution, including from its vast exports of coal and LNG that are among the highest in the world.
Lawyers behind the case are hoping for a resolution in the next 18 months. While a committee declaration is not legally binding, a negative finding would be a major embarrassment and would carry significant political weight.
“My Country is being fracked, our drinking water poisoned and our history erased as we speak,” said Dank.
She said the prime minister “needs to stop speaking and start listening to our brothers and sisters across the world when they say they don’t want us to export coal, oil or gas and the climate harms that they bring with them”.
Albanese had a series of bi-lateral meetings on the sidelines of Cop31 on Thursday with Bangladesh, Lebanon, Pacific leaders and the UK prime minister, Andy Burnham.

The UK and EU are set to strike a deal to help tackle post-Brexit shortages of medicines such as antibiotics, ADHD medication and epilepsy drugs at next week’s reset summit.



The two sides are finalising a health security agreement that will help address shortages of certain drugs which have got worse since Brexit, according to a draft text of a joint UK-EU statement seen by The i Paper.



The deal is designed to boost the sharing of intelligence on medicine supplies, helping the two sides collaborate as they experience supply shortages driven by global instability, but also partly by post-Brexit trade barriers in the case of the UK.



Experts on post-Brexit health policy said the planned deal appeared to be “significant” and a “good first step” in addressing shortages that have hit both sides of the Channel in recent years, with recent crises in obtaining medicines such antibiotics needed for winter illnesses, and critical products to help people with long-term conditions such as ADHD and epilepsy.



It is expected to come alongside a major Brexit reset package of agreements on food and drink trade, carbon markets and youth mobility that Andy Burnham said will boost the UK’s economy by adding 0.4 per cent to gross domestic product.



An EU draft text of a joint statement, which is forming a key part of the negotiations, refers to both sides using the 20 November summit in Brussels to welcome the signing of a memorandum of understanding on health security.

Full SummaryClimate activist Greta Thunberg criticized wealthy governments at the Cop31 summit in Antalya, Turkey, claiming they are failing to address the climate crisis. Leaders from Mali, Seychelles, and Palau also called for urgent action as nations at the frontline of the crisis face existential threats.
Climate activist Greta Thunberg has hit out at wealthy governments for not taking the climate crisis seriously enough, saying that the planet is “not dying, it is being killed and we know by who”. 
Speaking amid a throng of press on the sidelines of the UN’s Cop31 summit in Antalya, Turkey – the first time she has attended the conference in five years – she said that it is “being killed by the very same people thought to come to our rescue.” 
“No one is coming to our rescue... When our human rights are being threatened by states and other institutions, it’s our duty to stand up and be the adult in the room and fight for everyone’s human rights,” she added. 





The conference comes in a year marked by destructive weather events, including lethal floods and heatwaves, alongside energy market turbulence triggered by the Iran war.
It comes as nations at the frontline of the climate crisis – facing an existential threat – have called on larger countries to act now, as there is zero time to waste.

articles.jina_text:
Eighteen beaches in Kent have been closed due to an oil spill which the local council said will take "many days" to clean-up.
"Significant deposits of oil" were found at beaches across the Isle of Thanet, including Ramsgate and the popular tourist beaches of Margate and Broadstairs.
Thanet District Council (TDC) reported the incident on Wednesday evening and the Environmental Agency (EA) is investigating. The source of the oil has not been identified.
Mike Humber, director for the environment at the council, told BBC South East: "We never want to be saying to the public to not go on the beaches, but we have taken that decision to protect the public."
He added: "We want to clean up as quickly as we can. I think it will be many days, but it's difficult to be sure on that kind of timescale.
"It looks like its covering all of the beaches in Thanet. We need to think about public safety."





Image caption, 

Thanet District Council's director of environment said clean up of the oil deposits could take "many days"




East Thanet MP Polly Billington reiterated that "the source of this spill is unclear", but added that she was being kept up-to-date with developments and was "hoping to see our beautiful beaches reopened as quickly as possible".
A spokesperson for TDC urged people, particularly dog walkers, to avoid the affected areas, and to report any deposits of oil on beaches to the authority.
The council was working with the Maritime and Coastguard Agency to remove the deposits from all of the affected beaches, and that samples would be collected and analysed.
Coastguard aircraft have been flying over the affected area as part of the search.





Image caption, 

Oil deposits have been washing up on the shoreline




Early theories for the spill include a ship having washed out its engine, or the oil having come from a wreck which has broken up.
John Nichols, former chairman of the Thanet Fishermen's Association, said he thought the oil had "most likely come from a wartime wreck and engine fuel".
He said: "The oil looks old and breaks down easier. It won't take the coast guard long to discover where the oil has come from."
The reason it was ashore, he added, was "because of the wind direction and the high tides".
Local residents told the BBC conditions on Wednesday and Thursday were particularly windy.

Andy Burnham has clocked up more than 22,500 air miles on taxpayer-funded overseas flights in his first 115 days as Prime Minister, GB News can reveal.
Mr Burnham, whose jet has also flown around 1,000 miles within the UK, is close to being able to circle the world after touching down in Dublin for today's European Political Community summit.








The Prime Minister flew to the Irish capital straight from Turkey following a whistle-stop visit to Antalya for the Cop31 summit.
He flew almost 4,000 miles in 48 hours to deliver a 764-word speech, which averages out at five miles per word and 666 miles a minute.




Mr Burnham, the only G7 leader to attend the climate summit, spent just 14 hours on Turkish soil before jetting straight to Dublin.
The Prime Minister used his speech to declare the "climate crisis is not a distant threat", adding: "We're committed to meeting our 2050 net zero target and committed to working with all of our partners to reach theirs."
However, Mr Burnham's taxpayer-funded jet is estimated to have pumped out around 300 tonnes of CO2 since he took office.


The figure, based on the jet burning around 2,200kg of fuel an hour and each kilogram releasing just over three kilograms of CO2, is around 70 times the 4.53 tonnes the average Briton produces in a year.






Andy Burnham is the only G7 leader to attend Cop31 | GETTY

Full SummaryForeign Secretary Ed Miliband described billions in pledges for the Tropical Forest Forever Facility as a powerful signal of global momentum to protect forests. The initiative, which pays countries to conserve standing forest, has received support from both wealthy donors and developing nations like Indonesia and Brazil.
Billions of dollars in pledges for a high-profile forest protection fund from developing countries – and not just a small group of traditional donors with dwindling aid budgets – represents a ”powerful signal” of aid efforts to help the climate crisis, Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband has suggested. 
Mr Miliband made the comments to The Independent after a high profile event at Cop31 where countries reaffirmed commitments to the Tropical Forest Forever Facility (TFFF): a new forest finance initiative designed to pay tropical forest countries a recurring, performance-based amount per hectare of conserved standing forest.
Launched by President Lula at Cop30 in Brazil last year, the fund has now been promised £400m from the UK, $500m (£380m) from the Netherlands, and nearly $100m from climate philanthropies. 




Norway has promised to fund up to 20 per cent of the facility's initial $10 billion capitalisation target, and it is to receive $1bn from Indonesia and $1bn from Brazil: two rainforest nations that are also developing countries, and therefore do not typically face the same expectations as wealthier Western nations to provide aid
Speaking to The Independent after a period of sweeping aid cuts from developed countries including the UK, Mr Miliband commended the fact that a broader group of nations was supporting the fund.

Downing Street has defended Andy Burnham’s attendance at the Cop31 summit on a trip across two countries amid questions about whether the journey delivered value for money and reflected his net-zero ambitions.




No 10 said flying to Turkey for the climate conference and then to Ireland for the European Political Community (EPC) meeting was “absolutely” a good use of the Prime Minister’s time.








Scrutiny of Mr Burnham’s travel has heightened after a Government plane was flown from London to Manchester to pick him up on the way to a Commonwealth summit in the Caribbean last week, earning him the nickname Air Miles Andy among opponents.




Andy Burnham has said the UK is committed to meeting its 2050 net zero target and working with other countries to reach theirs.




The Prime Minister has so far made four international trips since entering office in July, to show support for Ukraine, to attend the UN general assembly in the US, to sign a defence treaty in Germany and his most recent to Antigua.




By the end of Thursday he will have visited two more countries – Turkey for the UN’s Cop31 gathering, where he delivered a five-minute speech pledging a “new era” of British leadership on the green transition, and Ireland for the EPC.




He was the first speaker at the climate conference on Thursday, addressing a half-empty plenary hall at the start of the session with Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband and London Mayor Lord Sadiq Khan in the audience.




Asked whether the Prime Minister thinks it was worth travelling to Turkey to deliver a brief speech to a half-empty room, a No 10 spokeswoman said: “So, obviously, the Prime Minister delivered his speech at Cop this morning, where he said we are committed to meeting our 2050 net-zero target and committed to working with all of our partners to reach theirs.












“He said that the climate crisis is not a distant threat; it is upon us all now, devastating lives and livelihoods everywhere.




“As the Prime Minister said in his speech this morning, climate leadership and action have become more urgent, and Britain will answer the call.”








Pressed on whether that meant No 10 thought it was a good use of time, she said: “Absolutely.”


Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s travel choices have been defended by Downing Street (Toby Melville/PA)
PA Wire




Asked whether flying to Turkey and then Ireland was a good use of taxpayer money and a good example to people for reaching net zero, the official said: “As I’ve said, the Prime Minister has been very clear that the climate crisis is no longer a distant threat and he feels that it’s extremely important to meet with other leaders and address to help address the key challenges posed by climate change.




“On the European Political Community meeting, as I set out, he will attend a number of meetings there, including on Ukraine, with the hope of making further progress towards a just and lasting peace there.”

articles.jina_text:
Addressing other world leaders and delegates at the COP31 climate summit in Turkey, he said that despite this, the UK was ready to begin a "new era of British leadership" on the climate change issue.
But environmental campaigners at the summit said the PM had to back up his warm words with stronger actions.
In recent months, the UK government has announced policies which critics say have weakened its green credentials, such as reducing support for heat pumps, approving the Jackdaw gas field and doubling down on support for Heathrow Airport's expansion.
Burnham opened his speech on Thursday by talking about the heat experienced in the UK this past summer.
He said "it was not normal" - in fact it was the hottest on record, made 130 times more likely because of climate change, according to the Met Office.
Hundreds of schools were closed, cereal harvests were down 11%, and ambulance services were inundated with calls beyond levels seen during the Covid-19 pandemic.
As a result of the threat to people's health and homes, the PM said he was creating the UK, and the world's, first climate security envoy, Dame Madeleine Alessandri.














Alessandri, the former head of the Joint Intelligence Committee, said: "Climate change and nature loss are increasingly shaping the security environment in which the UK operates."
As a result this was "placing additional pressure on resources, economies and communities around the world", she added.
This will be seen as a strong indication of the focus of the UK's priorities when it takes up the G20 presidency next year. 
The current president is the US, which has been a notable absentee from the COP process over the last two years since President Trump withdrew the country from the most important global climate treaty - the Paris Climate Agreement.
Professor Lord Nicholas Stern, who identified 20 years ago that climate change could cost the global economy up to 20% of GDP if left unchecked, praised the PM's words.
"The Prime Minister was right to identify climate change as a threat to security around the world, and the importance of investments in clean electricity generation as the best way of protecting households and businesses from the high prices and volatile markets for fossil fuels," he said.

Christopher Furlong/Getty Images
Homes in the West Midlands were destroyed after record wildfires this summer in the UK
On tackling the causes of climate change, Burnham said his government remained committed to meeting the country's target of net zero by 2050 whilst also getting bills down.










He said key to this was cutting our "dependence on fossil fuels" and increasing electrification - the amount of our energy needs met from renewable electricity.
The main driver of rising global temperatures has been the increasing concentration of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere, largely caused by burning fossil fuels.

Trump the ‘biggest loser’ for scrapping climate action, John Kerry says at Cop31


Kerry decries president for ceding clean-energy dominance to China and says climate crisis still a key issue for voters




Donald Trump is the “biggest loser we’ve seen in a long time” for scrapping action on the climate crisis and ceding the clean energy race to China, former US secretary of state John Kerry has said.






Cop31 may involve lots of talking about talking – but there are wins to be had

Read more

Kerry, speaking at the Cop31 climate summit in Turkey, criticized Trump for withdrawing the US from the international climate process and axing measures that reduced planet-heating emissions. Unlike almost all other countries in the world, the Trump administration has sent no delegation to the resort city of Antalya for the annual UN climate talks, which started on Monday.
The US president, who has previously called climate science a “hoax” and called for countries to drill for more oil and gas, again expressed his hostility towards clean energy on Monday. “I will not approve wind turbines because wind turbines are a major loser,” Trump, who has long-held animus towards wind farms, said about potential new legislation that would make it easier to build new energy projects.
Asked about his comments by the Guardian, Kerry said: “[The] first thing they should do is hold up a really big mirror so he can look at a loser, because he’s the biggest loser we’ve seen in a long time on all of these issues.”
“He’s missing the point,” Kerry, a former climate envoy for Joe Biden’s administration, added. “He’s missing the competitiveness with China. He’s missing the marketplace for goods that could be produced in the United States. We could be the supply chain for some of these.”
Under Biden, the US passed sweeping climate legislation that gave tax breaks for clean energy and electric vehicle manufacturing in a bid to compete with China, which has dominated clean tech.
Republicans eliminated most of this support, however, with Trump instead imposing tariffs on various goods and pouring public money into propping up struggling coal-fired power plants. Coal is the dirtiest of fossil fuels, causing much of the pollution that is dangerously overheating our planet.
“He declared he wanted to beat China, be number one in X, Y, or Z, and he walked away from the battlefield,” Kerry said of Trump. “He totally took America out of that sector. So honestly, if you want to be number one, you don’t do it by literally blackballing an entire sector of the economy.”

articles.jina_text:
A cluster of candy cane-striped smoke stacks dots the horizon of Tufts Cove in Nova Scotia, Canada. Deep in the briny depths of Halifax harbour, something huge is happening: the ocean is being engineered to remove atmospheric carbon.
“This is what Mother Nature has done naturally for a few billion years in order to rebalance the atmospheric and ocean chemistry over long timescales,” says Dr Greg Rau, co-founder and senior scientist at Planetary Technologies.

Planetary Technologies is an ocean carbon-removal firm and one of a growing number of companies attempting to decrease excess atmospheric carbon – the main driver of the climate crisis – by speeding up naturally occurring carbon cycles in the ocean.
To do this, the company conducts ocean alkalinity enhancement (OAE), adding a chalk-like substance to the seawater, which allows the water to absorb and store more atmospheric carbon than usual.

Ocean alkalinity enhancement works by dissolving alkaline minerals to increase the seawater’s pH, which leads to carbon dioxide being drawn down into the ocean
This process also helps to offset ocean acidification, often called the “evil twin” of the climate crisis, which is increasing dramatically.
Because it relies on an already occurring process, proponents say these technologies will not harm the marine creatures that call this harbour home, such as mackerel, sunfish, harbour seals and sea turtles. But some marine scientists worry that adding any extra materials to an already stressed ecosystem might harm aquatic life and say that this field of marine geoengineering needs more research.
“If we develop a new medicine, you have steps that you’re supposed to take. You don’t just find a substance and just implement it,” says Sam Dupont, a senior lecturer at the University of Gothenburg. “And at the moment, with [ocean carbon removal] it seems you’re jumping to clinical trial immediately.”
Planetary Technologies runs its operations five days a week. Working out of a shipping container, it adds an alkaline slurry, its proprietary formula, to a local power company’s cooling water to create an odourless milky composite, which is then discharged into Halifax harbour and monitored by their sensors.
Bolstered initially by small government grants, venture funds and other private capital, Planetary Technologies now generates revenue by selling carbon-removal credits worth millions of dollars to companies such as JPMorgan Chase and Shopify.
Ocean carbon removal is a fledgling industry but one that has seen more than $500m (£370m) invested since 2021, according to Ocean Carbon Removal Watch, a database launched by the Pulitzer Center, which tracks marine carbon dioxide removal (mCDR) investments.

articles.title: Burnham commits to 2050 net zero target and working with others to reach theirs
articles.raw_rss: The Prime Minister pledged a ‘new era of British leadership over the next decade’ on the climate.
articles.raw_meta: The Prime Minister pledged a ‘new era of British leadership over the next decade’ on the climate.
articles.jina_text:
Andy Burnham has said “Britain is back and ready to play its full part” in tackling climate change in a “new era” of leadership over the next decade as he addressed the UN Cop31 summit in Turkey.




Amid accusations that his Government is deprioritising the green agenda, the Prime Minister recommitted to hitting its 2050 net zero target and to working with other countries to reach theirs.








Attending the annual climate gathering for the first time as Prime Minister on Thursday, he warned that the “climate crisis is upon all of us now” after a “not normal” summer of extreme heat, wildfires and drought.




“The climate crisis is not a distant threat; it is upon us all now, devastating lives and livelihoods everywhere,” he said.




Andy Burnham has said the UK is committed to meeting its 2050 net zero target and working with other countries to reach theirs.




“Meanwhile, two wars across two continents have sent fuel prices and gas bills soaring for families and businesses across the world. The common thread running through all of this: our dependence on fossil fuels.




“The message I carry here at my first Cop as UK Prime Minister is this: we’re committed to meeting our 2050 net zero target, and committed to working with all of our partners to reach theirs.”




Mr Burnham is expected to be the only G7 leader to address the summit in the Mediterranean resort city of Antalya, with US President Donald Trump declining to send a delegation for the second year running.












He was the first speaker at the conference on Thursday, addressing a half-empty plenary hall at the start of the session with Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband and London Mayor Lord Sadiq Khan in the audience.




“Britain will live up to its commitments. We will help our friends as they live up to theirs. Britain is back and ready to play its full part,” Mr Burnham said.








As the world will overshoot 1.5C warming above pre-industrial levels this century – a central target of the Paris Agreement – “climate leadership and action have become more urgent”, the Labour leader said.




“Britain will answer the call. Climate is a national security issue.”




As part of these efforts, Dame Madeleine Alessandri, former chairwoman of the Joint Intelligence Committee which provides ministers with national security assessments, has been appointed special representative for climate security, the Prime Minister said.


Andy Burnham told the conference that Britain is ready ‘to play its full part’ (Stefan Rousseau/PA)
PA Wire




Calling on industry leaders to “play their part” to help people on all incomes make the green transition, Mr Burnham said: “This crisis can only be solved in partnership. I have pledged a new era of British leadership over the next decade.

articles.title: 'Summer was a wake-up call, winter could be dire' warning over food supplies
articles.raw_rss: Wales needs to grow more fruit and veg or it will be at the mercy of wars and climate change, one expert says.
articles.raw_meta: Wales needs to grow more fruit and veg or it will be at the mercy of wars and climate change, one expert says.
articles.jina_text:
Droughts and wildfires in the summer were a wake-up call, and winter flooding could leave Wales' food supply vulnerable, an expert has warned.
The country currently imports the vast majority of its fruit and vegetables, with only 6% of those served in its schools grown in Wales.
It is dependent on produce from parts of the world prone to droughts and fires, according to co-founder of an organisation aiming to address this. 
Duncan Fisher is behind Our Food Trust, external, which wants to build 100 farms, producing fruit and vegetables in Wales for local markets.
Despite 90% of the country being used for agriculture, external, only about 0.1% is currently being used for horticulture, external.
Growers at Fisher's Wern Farm, near Newtown, Powys, said this must change if the country is to survive climate change, wars and other global disruptions to the supply chain.
"We are hugely dependent and these vegetables are coming from really vulnerable parts of the world like south Europe and north Africa - the areas most prone to drought, fires and overheating," said Fisher.
Food security has become a hot topic, with Defence Secretary Wes Streeting saying in October people should have water, tinned goods, baby food, torches and mobile phone charging packs ready in case of emergency.
Fisher referenced this appeal, adding the UK "has an incredibly centralised food system with 95% of the food we eat bought from nine supermarkets".
He said: "There's no storage, it's a just-in-time system so the food is stored in lorries moving across motorways.
"That is a security hazard because it's very vulnerable to cyber-attacks.
"If the system goes wrong, there's no resilience in it. The food just runs out straight away."




Image source, Duncan Fisher
Image caption, 

Duncan Fisher said he has hope that Wales will be able to increase its fruit and veg growing




Fisher and Sue Holbrook launched Our Food Trust about 10 years ago with the aim of growing more produce locally for local markets.
They found one of the main barriers was stable housing for farmers.
As Fisher explained: "If there's a high wind during the night, they need to get out there and protect things.
"If a sheep gets in, they have to get the sheep out before the entire thing is destroyed in an hour. So they have to live there."
But he said planning regulations have made it really difficult to build homes on farmland.
However, by working with Powys council and Bannau Brycheiniog National Park Authority, they have been able to build three temporary homes for farmers on 36 acres of council-owned land.
They are currently building three more.




Image source, Lydia Dibben
Image caption, 

Lydia Dibben, one of the growers, said even though it was a difficult year they were able to grow a lot of food




One of the growers at Wern Farm is Lydia Dibben, 28, and she agreed access to land is one of the biggest barriers to new farmers.

World heading for ‘irrevocable overshoot’ of global temperature thresholds, analysis warns


Failure to cut emissions will ‘consign humanity to disasters they are unable to adapt to’, report says




The world is heading for an “irrecoverable overshoot” of global temperature thresholds that will plunge billions of people into disastrous climate impacts because governments have stalled for so long to cut planet-heating emissions, analysis has found.
Under current policies, the planet will heat up by 2.7C on average by the end of the century compared with preindustrial times, the report by Climate Action Tracker (CAT) found. This is up slightly from a prediction of 2.6C in the group’s analysis conducted last year.

This level of warming smashes the 1.5C threshold that was agreed by countries a decade ago but is set to be breached in just a few years. Scientists have warned that beyond this point already harmful storms, droughts, heatwaves, flooding and other impacts will become intolerable for parts of the world and potentially trigger runaway climate change that won’t be contained.







‘My classroom was 30C. No one was learning. Then I started to feel dizzy’ – This is climate breakdown

Read more
Countries, minus the US, are gathered in the Turkish city of Antalya for UN climate talks that have centred on the looming “overshoot” of the temperature target. This reality should compel governments to act quickly to phase out use of the fossil fuels that are causing the climate crisis, the UN secretarygeneral, António Guterres, said on Tuesday.
If countries did act decisively to slash emissions then the future temperature projections would become less daunting, the CAT report states. However, in even the most optimistic scenario – where all pledges, targets and other long-term promises made by countries were fulfilled – the world would still heat up by 1.9C by the end of the century.
Such targets have been routinely flouted by the countries that have made them, however. This means leaders face a crunch moment, experts say.


“The stark choice for governments is to either continue to support the fossil fuel industry, which would consign humanity to insurmountable economic damages, rising mortality from heat and climate-driven diseases and disasters that they are unable to adapt to – or pivot to the solutions which are available and cheaper than ever,” says Bill Hare, chief executive of CAT partner organisation Climate Analytics.
